articles.title: Nvidia’s DLSS 5, explained
articles.summary: Nvidia’s DLSS 5 is arriving on September 3rd in its first game. Here’s how the tech works, based on unofficial hands-on and an official briefing.
articles.body: Nvidia knows that DLSS 5 left a bad first impression. In March, many gamers took one look at Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft’s DLSS 5-ified face and declared it AI slop. So this week, the company’s re-introducing its controversial “neural rendering” with firm messaging about how it “preserves artistic intent,” “respects the rendered frame,” and gives game developers full control. Now, ahead of its September 3rd launch, with an official Nvidia briefing under our belt and some hands-on time with the version that leaked onto the web, we think we finally get the picture. Here’s what’s going on. Is DLSS 5 AI slop? The critics weren’t wrong: DLSS 5 largely is a generative AI filter for video games. Kind of like a camera filter on your phone, DLSS 5 analyzes and modifies a real-time stream of 2D images after your 3D game engine is done spitting them out. It can indeed make game characters look terrible if applied poorly, like they’ve aged 20 years in a split-second. It uses a lot of GPU power, and can easily cut framerate in half — even applied well, you could argue that existing games look better without it. But DLSS 5 isn’t what we typically think of when we think of generative AI. It doesn’t change shapes, or hallucinate words on a sign, or place brand-new fake objects in view. Instead, it imagines light, shadow, color, and detail that make the same shapes appear differently. [Image: DLSS 5 can make dull, pasty characters look far more photorealistic. It can fill their hair and clothing and nearby foliage with signs of realistic light. It can ground characters and objects and clothing so they don’t look like they’re floating above video game surfaces. Here’s an example I captured myself in Yakuza Kiwami: with DLSS on, see how contact shadows underneath each character make them seem like they’re actually standing on the ground? [Image: [Image: (Later in this story, you should really check out how Cade Cunningham’s jersey casts shadows on his video game body, so it looks more like he’s wearing it.) And unlike AI-generated photos and videos, that usually produce different results with the same prompt, Nvidia claims DLSS 5 is deterministic, so games should look the same every time. DLSS 5 is also not one-size-fits-all. Despite what it sounds like, “DLSS 5 On” and “DLSS 5 Off” isn’t just an on-off switch. Developers (and apparently modders) can drag various sliders to change how DLSS 5 plays with color and light, and they have three different AI models to work with at launch, giving your graphics “default,” “natural” or “cinematic” looks. Plus, developers can decide whether to apply DLSS 5 to everything in a scene, just a character’s face and skin, just foliage, just silverware or furniture or even just food. You’re saying game studios could leave character faces alone? Yep. The toolset can automatically cut out a mask, like in Photoshop, to isolate a character’s face and skin from everything else: [Image: The automated mask precisely selects this character’s face, so game developers can enhance it — or make sure it’s left alone. If they don’t like the automated mask, devs can cut one out themselves. That’s the little “Developer Masking” checkbox in the image above. “There’s no limit to how many masks, how many groups, they could implement,” says Nvidia’s director of real-time content technology Gabriele Leone. Would game studios actually leave the faces alone? Probably not! The first game brave enough to ship with the tech is NBA 2K27, and I suspect that’s because Cade Cunningham actually looks a bit better with detailed skin, a uniform that doesn’t seem glued to his body, and a bit more glint in his eye. Take a look at Nvidia’s images for yourself: [Image: [Image: That basketball, too — doesn’t it feel a bit more lifelike now most of its detail is in shadow? But what about DLSStelle and all the other horrific AI faces I’ve seen since modders got hold of the tech? [Media: Truly deranged. But these games are supposed to look like animation, and surely their creators would never do anything like this to them, right? Right?? “The soul and goal of GeForce is to achieve photorealism in real-time rendering,” Nvidia’s director of applied deep learning Edward Liu told journalists. And games with more realistic art styles don’t look anywhere near this bad. But even realistic games can look wrong if the sliders are set too aggressively. What do you mean by “too aggressively?” I’m willing to bet that if you’ve seen the leaked DLSS 5 modifying an existing game, the unofficial DLSS 5 mod was set to its default level of around 80 percent intensity or even higher. Some creators will even pump it up to 200 percent to make the difference between “DLSS on” and “DLSS off” especially clear. But I believe even 80 percent is far too aggressive for many existing games. It can feel like you’re artificially aging a character by weathering their skin and deepening the wrinkles and creases in their face. To show you, I fired up Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Here’s what Lara Croft looks like with DLSS 5 at 0 percent, 80 percent, and 200 percent intensity: [Image: [Image: [Image: She seems… weathered, no? But at 40 percent intensity, she still looks like the same video game character to me, only with a bit more life in her eyes: [Image: [Image: Similarly, here’s Kazuma Kiryu from Yakuza Kiwami once more. In this part of the game, he’s supposed to be 27 years old, and nowhere near the grizzled veteran he is by Yakuza 6. But as I ramp up the intensity from 0 to 40 to 85 percent, you can see his furrowed brow gets more furrowed, his hair lightens, and the increased shadow across his cheeks makes his face appear slightly gaunt. [Image: [Image: [Image: He looks older — even if the underlying geometry of his face hasn’t actually changed. In a cutscene at 85 percent, it even looks like his hair might be tinged with grey: [Image: Does this look like a 27-year-old man to you? But again, it’s something developers and modders can control with some granularity. I’d probably enjoy a version of DLSS 5 for older games that ignores the faces but enhances a character’s gear. Kiryu’s sworn brother and antagonist Majima, below, doesn’t quite look right to me — but his eyepatch and necklace look excellent. [Image: [Image: By the way, these are just me playing with the overarching DLSS 5 slider when set to its “default” model. There are actually three different AI models, each with a slightly different look, and two different sliders, one for “tone” and one for “structure.” What’s the difference? I’m telling myself that “tone” is about light and color, while “structure” is about shadows and definition. But it’s probably easier to show you by isolating each: [Image: [Image: [Image: Officially, Nvidia says that “structure intensity” controls a mix of ambient occlusion, contact shadows, reflections and subsurface scattering (read: how light scatters through materials like hair, skin, and leaves), while “tone intensity” controls color and “broader lighting” details. [Image: What about the three different AI models? Nvidia only called them Model A, Model B and Model C in my briefing, but the DLSS 5 mod I used describes them as “default,” “cinematic” and “natural.” Here’s the image Nvidia provided to show the difference: [Image: Nvidia’s three AI looks. And here’s my own comparison in Shadow of the Tomb Raider — you may need to blow these up and cycle through to spot the differences. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Is this really an AI filter? It doesn’t use the game engine at all? Nvidia says that DLSS 5 can take some cues from game engines. But it’s based on the colors and motion vectors that it sees in the flat 2D frames, after they’re rendered and after other techniques like DLSS Super Resolution are applied. When we asked how DLSS 5 knows the difference between a character model, an object, and a piece of foliage, Liu replied that the model was trained to recognize what it sees. “Just like a person, if you look at anything, you know where things are.” You can even technically run DLSS 5 on video capture from a Nintendo Switch 2, and modders have already found ways to inject it into earlier games that used OpenGL and DirectX 9. Will game developers actually buy into DLSS 5? Will they use it well? That’s one of the big remaining questions — and one that Nvidia left unanswered during and after our briefing. While Nvidia said in March that DLSS 5 would come to at least 16 different games including Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, and Resident Evil Requiem, the company did not answer questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor did it confirm that other titles are still coming following the original backlash. Perhaps Nvidia and its partners will wait and see how reviewers and gamers react first. It’s worth noting that this may be a niche technology to start: while it no longer requires two RTX 5090 GPUs to function, it still uses a lot of horsepower. Officially, DLSS 5 is only coming to the latest RTX 50 series GPUs, which have become quite expensive: even a lower-mid-range RTX 5060 retailers for around $470 these days. Nvidia claims that an RTX 5060 is enough to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ultra settings, ray tracing, and DLSS 5 enabled — assuming you’re pairing it with a fast gaming CPU and a whole heap of RAM. [Image: These framerates are with 6x frame-gen enabled, so divide by six to get a better idea of how responsive the game might feel. Just how much of a performance hit are we talking? With NBA 2K27, Nvidia claims the performance hit is 50 to 60 percent on average across all Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs. When I ran the Shadow of the Tomb Raider benchmark at 1440p with on an RTX 5090 at Highest spec, DLSS Quality and an unofficial DLSS 5 mod, I saw framerate exactly cut in half — 312fps with DLSS 5 off, 156fps with it on. Will gamers be able to tweak DLSS 5 the way they like? The DLSS 5 mods are so easy to apply, it seems like the cat is out of the bag. But Nvidia’s message is that the developer has full control, and it didn’t answer questions about whether it’ll provide controls to gamers, too. Which mod should I install? I don’t yet feel comfortable recommending one — there’s been a feeding frenzy for DLSS 5 mods ever since the leak and we haven’t been able to properly vet. I installed one on a completely fresh system, just in case something went wrong. How have gamers reacted to Nvidia’s re-introduction of DLSS 5 so far? The reactions have been all over the place since DLSS 5 leaked and modders began posting their work. I’ve seen people say that DLSS 5 looks like a free next-gen remaster of any game you like, and I’ve seen people say it looks as terrible as it did before. I’ve seen people suggest that even if it looks good, it’ll make every game look too similar once developers start using it as a crutch. But many of those impressions were based on images and videos of the tech at its extremes. Once people realize there’s granular control, perhaps reactions will become more measured. Correction: An earlier version of this article misidentified characters in screenshots; they are NBA player Cade Cunningham and Majima from Yakuza.

articles.title: Nvidia’s controversial DLSS 5 arrives September 3rd and requires serious GPU horsepower
articles.summary: Nvidia is officially launching DLSS 5 this week following a divisive announcement in March. The first game that supports it is NBA 2K27.
articles.body: Nvidia is officially launching DLSS 5 this week, following a divisive announcement in March where we likened the AI upscaling tech to a “real-time generative AI filter for video games” and “motion smoothing for video games, but worse.” DLSS 5 will officially be available on RTX 50-series desktop and laptop GPUs and through GeForce Now cloud gaming, though the only game with the tech so far is NBA 2K27 — which is launching September 3rd at 9PM PT on PC. When it was announced, Nvidia lauded DLSS 5 as “the company’s most significant breakthrough in computer graphics since the debut of real-time ray tracing in 2018,” and highlighted how the tech uses AI to make games look more realistic by enhancing a game based on its source content. Nvidia also stressed that DLSS 5 gave developers controls that let them decide how changes from DLSS 5 appeared in their games. [Image: [Image: Image compare: drag the handle to see the difference Nvidia says it can provide in NBA 2K27. Tap here for full-res with DLSS 5 off, and with DLSS 5 on. But accompanying examples shared by Nvidia were widely criticized and meme’d on for significantly changing how characters looked, such as the “yassification” of Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft. With the official launch, Requiem still doesn’t support DLSS 5, and neither do other games shown in the March reveal, including EA Sports FC, Starfield, and Hogwarts Legacy, so we don’t know how the final version of the tech might now appear in those titles. Nvidia did not answer our questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor reconfirm that previously confirmed titles will still include the tech. [Image: Tap, twice, for higher res versions. [Image: Tap, twice, for higher res versions. In examples from NBA 2K27 we saw in a press briefing, though, changes from DLSS 5 don’t appear to be quite as dramatic as the types of adjustments shown in the initial reveal. The shadows and textures added by DLSS 5 generally made the players in the game look more realistic instead of turning them into AI caricatures. You can see more in our deeper dive here. In briefings, Nvidia showed how developers will have many sliders at their disposal to determine exactly how much DLSS 5 changes things, and that developers can choose to amp up whichever parts of the scene they prefer. They can even leave characters’ faces alone and just enhance silverware or food or foliage, Nvidia says. [Image: [Image: Image slider: drag the handle to make bacon look more real by giving it shadows. While Nvidia’s original DLSS 5 demos required a pair of RTX 5090 gaming graphics cards, the company claims even a single midrange RTX 5060 can manage to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ray tracing and DLSS 5 at ultra spec — if you have one of he fastest gaming CPUs and enable 6x frame generation (meaning the game is only producing one “real” frame for every six frames you see). DLSS 5 is still a huge performance hit. Nvidia estimates it at 50 to 60 percent, and we saw performance cut in half when we tried an unofficial DLSS5 mod in Shadow of the Tomb Raider. [Image: So far, Nvidia has shown us examples that demonstrate the ideal version of what’s possible with DLSS 5 (and promote NBA 2K27). We haven’t yet tested an official build of DLSS 5 ourselves to get an idea of how the tech might look, but we have tried the unofficial version that modders are using to mess with older games like Control and Skyrim. With older games, it seems, a little sprinkle of DLSS 5 goes a long way.

articles.title: Afterworld: The First Hands-On Preview: A (Probably Too Early) Taste of Paradox’s Next Big Thing
articles.summary: Typical for a Paradox game, Afterworld contains systems upon systems upon systems. It would be impossible to cover them all in the scope of this preview, from sending ranger teams into devastated cities to recover old-world tech, to equipping armies with bikes and dune buggies to bring road war to the wasteland while having to maintain supply lines for fuel and ammo. It's a lot to come to grips with and, like I said, in need of a lot of polish and balancing.
articles.body:
The build I was shown was exceptionally early – shockingly so.

There are systems upon systems upon systems, as you’d expect from Paradox.

The Ancients are perhaps the most fascinating folk you’ll encounter in the wasteland.

I don't know about you, but my plans for the apocalypse involve hiding in a comfy bunker and playing hundreds of hours more of Paradox grand strategy games like Crusader Kings 3. And now I'll be able to play out the apocalypse during the apocalypse with the studio’s first new grand strategy game franchise since 2019's Imperator: Rome, Afterworld. Set in a not too far future North America that has been devastated by an intentionally vague cataclysm, it combines RTS and grand strategy elements as you rebuild the world in any image you desire – from terraforming to cannibalism. And that's an enticing proposition.

Heads up: what you're seeing is an alpha, and there were several things that we weren't allowed to show yet, like combat. It's undeniably rough around the edges. Honestly, one of my first thoughts was that this seems really early to be showing Afterworld to the public. There is a general shape of a game here, where you settle the wasteland, interact with rival factions, and deal with simmering internal conflict inside your own borders. But a lot of it really doesn't work yet and the balance is all over the place. And that’s OK of course; games are difficult and time-consuming to make. But just keep that in mind as I discuss what I saw.

I was told by the devs that they were getting it in our hands now so they could collect feedback while they still have time to act on it, before systems get fully baked. And I get that. But I will have to be kind of brutally honest that the build I played wasn't in a shape where I'd want to spend hundreds of hours with it. I hope they take all the time they need to make it the best it can be. I'd be a little bit concerned to hear they were planning to release this any earlier than Q4 next year.

But with that important caveat out of the way, let's take a step back and talk about what Afterworld actually is. It begins with selecting an origin for your starting band of survivors, similar to Stellaris. And if you've played other Paradox games, that's definitely the closest point of comparison. Just like ships in that game can fly around within a system, your military units and explorers – called rangers – have exact positions within the map's many provinces and can maneuver and fight individually.

The only origin that was available in this preview was the Shelterborn, who are basically Vault Dwellers from Fallout: having hidden underground for the last 100 years or so, they are now forced to deal with a surface world they know nothing about after their life support systems start to fail. The circumstances around which we left the shelter were played out in a brief choose-your-own-adventure-style sequence that can differentiate your new society as anything from nostalgic reclaimers seeking to restore Old America to bloodthirsty cannibals who see strangers as dinner. This sets your starting traditions, values, and customs.

Traditions are sort of a band's base stats, or how good they are at various aspects of post-apocalyptic state-building. Survival helps with the short-term task of simply not dying in the unforgiving surface world as you scrabble for resources. Hearthkeeping is more about making a nice place to live in the long term.

Values represent a band's feelings about certain ideologies: Reclamation is about rebuilding America as it was (or as they imagine it was based on legends). Wanderlust is about maintaining a nomadic lifestyle rather than settling down, which is fully possible in Afterworld as base settlements and certain buildings can be packed up and relocated. A band might feel positively, negatively, or not care about any number of the dozens of existing values.

Finally, customs are the story-based explanations of where your traditions and values come from. The Nostalgic custom, for instance, makes you feel positively about Reclamation and gives you a small bonus to Hearthkeeping. A band gains more customs over time either through accumulating pride, which works more or less like experience points, or by developing traumas as the result of negative events like losing a war or being struck by a disaster. Afterworld is an absolute soup of similar nouns, but you can basically get by remembering that traditions are what your band can do, values are how your band feels, and customs are how you acquire both of the above.

If you want to tame the wasteland, however, you'll have to eventually recruit or conquer more bands that come with their own set of values that may conflict with your own, impacting the larger tribe's cohesion and potentially causing a crisis if you can't make everyone get along. While bands that have food, water, and medical care can grow on their own, assimilating more bands is the only way of acquiring more labor quickly to collect resources, work in your fledgling industries, wage war, and eventually run your logistics network.

This quickly spirals into setting up a government with different bands divided between ruling elites, fully-enfranchised citizens, the oppressed underclass, and if your values allow it, maybe even slaves. I had the option to keep the shelter overseer in charge of everything or try to establish a democracy, and went for the latter path.

All the while, my rangers were out exploring the devastated provinces of the US Southeast. Radiation is a constant threat, especially near ruined cities. But you might also run into hostile clans of slavers, rogue war drones who see you as enemy combatants, bloodthirsty mutants, or simply other tribes competing for resources. The story implies that the world ended a fair bit later than where we are in 2026, so the types of technology you might rediscover in the ruins includes stuff like nanotech, combat mechs, and other sci-fi spectacles.

The biggest players in the wasteland, though, are the towering Ancients. The last survivors of the pre-fall world, each has found some way to prolong their life unnaturally, and each has a unique goal called a destiny that they seek to enact. The first one I ran into, Farouk the American, wants to restore the United States in his image as president of presidents, spreading his civic religion across the wasteland and preparing for a great election to legitimize his power. Lily of the Parks can be found in the Rocky Mountain region and is trying to reverse the ecological devastation humankind wrought. And that sounds nice as long as you don't ask where she's getting the fertilizer.

Fairly early on – probably a bit too early for my taste – I was given an ultimatum by Farouk to either become his subject or be forcibly subjugated. It's not really possible to beat him back in the early game, though you do have the option to pack up and move to New Hampshire where he might never bother you again. Joining him isn't all bad, though, as your tribe can rise through the ranks to become one of his lieutenants or captains, with each tier unlocking new perks. You just have to be prepared to pay tribute and sometimes do his dirty work. If you play your cards right, you may be able to contest his sham election and put forth your own leader to become president.

Typical for a Paradox game, Afterworld contains systems upon systems upon systems. It would be impossible to cover them all in the scope of this preview, from sending ranger teams into devastated cities to recover old-world tech, to equipping armies with bikes and dune buggies to bring road war to the wasteland while having to maintain supply lines for fuel and ammo. It's a lot to come to grips with and, like I said, in need of a lot of polish and balancing. But I'll be keeping this one in my sights, not least of which for the fascinating premise and the ability to fulfill my dream of running an anarcho-primitivist pagan warrior cult in the Rocky Mountains.

articles.title: Marvel’s Wolverine: Explaining the Origins of the PS5 Game’s Suits
articles.summary: We break down every costume confirmed to appear in Marvel's Wolverine and how Insomniac's new game draws on decades of X-Men lore.
articles.body:
Just like with the various Spider-Man games, half the fun of Marvel's Wolverine is getting to pick from literally dozens of different costume choices as you hack and claw your way across the Marvel Universe. Insomniac has clearly done its homework, as they've crammed in plenty of suits inspired by classic Marvel Comics storylines, and even some from the various X-Men cartoons and movies. All that, plus they found room to include a few original designs, to boot.

As we count down the final days until Marvel's Wolverine hits the PS5, let's explore every costume confirmed to appear in the game and how it pays homage to the source material.

Marvel's Wolverine: Every Costume in the PS5 Game

Much like Marvel's Spider-Man, Marvel's Wolverine focuses on a core costume that, while it pays homage to the comics, also stands as an original creation by the designers at Insomniac. In this case, Insomniac has dubbed Logan's new suit the "Battle Reborn" costume. It's clearly based on Wolverine's classic yellow and blue Tiger Stripe and Astonishing costumes, but it's also been given a more rugged and functional overhaul. It's a tool more than a visual statement, befitting a universe where the X-Men as we know them don't yet exist.

The game features a number of suits where Wolverine trades in his bright yellow spandex for more ordinary civilian clothes. None of these are necessarily a 1:1 copy of any specific comic book look, but all speak to Logan's particular fashion sense - cowboy hats, leather jackets, tank tops, and so forth.

This armored suit is inspired by the one Logan wore in the 2013 Wolverine comic. At the time, his healing factor had been shorted out, forcing him to rely on a flexible yet impervious costume with its own built-in set of claws.

1995's Age of Apocalypse crossover introduced an alternate Marvel timeline where Professor Xavier was killed as a young man and Apocalypse awoke early, ushering in a new dystopian era. Like his fellow X-Men, Wolverine is a dramatically different person in this reality, reflected by his red and blue costume and the fact that he's missing his left hand (the claws remain, though).

2004's Astonishing X-Men #1 ended the X-Men's flirtation with black leather costumes and brought back the spandex look. Artist John Cassaday redesigned Logan's classic Tiger Stripe costume for a new era, playing around with the shapes and establishing a new look that would remain the gold standard for the next 10 years.

If any comic book outfit can rival the Tiger Stripe costume as Logan's most iconic look, it's this one. It was introduced way back in 1980's Uncanny X-Men #139 and stuck around for the next decade. The Brown Costume has inspired many suits that have followed, and Wolverine still returns to this look every now and again.

2024's Deadpool & Wolverine not only marked the official MCU debut of both characters, it was also the first time Hugh Jackman was seen wearing a truly comics-accurate costume with a mask. This MCU suit is heavily inspired by the Astonishing X-Men costume from the comics, though it introduced a pair of sleeves for good measure (at least until they were ripped away in the climax of the film).

Uncanny X-Men #107 marked one of the first times Wolverine was given a drastic visual makeover in the comics. After his standard costume was damaged in battle, Logan stole an orange and red suit worn by a Shi'ar Imperial Guardian known as Fang. It was a taste of what was to come with his beloved brown costume.

Marvel's Wolverine isn't the only new game to feature the Ol' Canucklehead this year. He's also a playable character in the fighting game Marvel Tokon. That costume, with its bold, cel-shaded style and bombastic take on the Astonishing X-Men design, has been ported over to Marvel's Wolverine.

With 2000's X-Men movie revitalizing interest in the franchise, Marvel Comics responded by ditching the X-Men's classic spandex costumes and outfitting them in more functional black leather outfits. With these Frank Quitely-designed costumes, the yellow X logo became a form of branding, every bit as potent as a Nike swoosh symbol.

2009's Old Man Logan storyline introduced a futuristic version of the Marvel Universe where the world's villains banded together to finally defeat their enemies. Wolverine, now an aging, disgraced farmer with a family to protect, abandoned his classic costume for a more Wild West-inspired getup. The game adapts that look, specifically the version with the full trenchcoat.

Wolverine made his debut as a Hulk villain in 1974's The Incredible Hulk #181 before quickly going on to become a star in the pages of Uncanny X-Men. Artist John Romita, Sr.'s original costume design isn't that far off from the classic Tiger Stripe look that would become so iconic, but a few details were different. Most notably, this early design featured unusual whiskers on the mask.

Marvel celebrated Wolverine's first ongoing solo comic in 1988 with the debut of a drastically different costume. This stealthy number ditched all the color in favor of an all-black approach. Even black face paint was used to help mask Logan's identity during his time in Madripoor.

Long before he was a member of the X-Men, Logan served on a black ops mutant strikeforce known as Team X. That backstory looks to play a key role in the game, so it's only fitting that Marvel's Wolverine would include this memorable costume. Just as in the comics, it combines a functional black bodysuit with plenty of bold yellow padding.

Marvel's second incarnation of the Ultimate Universe is one where a villain known as The Maker systematically interfered with the origins of countless heroes, creating a world very different from the Marvel Universe we know and love. Here, Logan is the Winter Soldier, a Russian super-soldier who sports an unusual costume marked by a large red star and a full face mask.

In the early '00s, Marvel went through a period where they wanted Wolverine to have the same look across all media. The result was this "Unified Costume," a more muted black suit with yellow tiger stripes on the shoulders. This look appeared in both the regular Marvel Universe and the Ultimate Universe, as well as in the animated series X-Men Evolution.

No costume lineup would be complete without Wolverine's Weapon X look. This is how he looked when he was captured by Weapon X and subjected to the adamantium bonding process, complete with copious amounts of tubes and wires and a bulky VR helmet.

During Jim Lee's beloved tenure on Uncanny X-Men, the team went through a brief phase where every X-Man wore the same blue and yellow costume. Logan was no exception. This matchy-matchy look didn't last long, though Banshee would continue to wear his school uniform for a couple of years.

Following the events of 2008's Messiah Complex crossover, Cyclops reformed X-Force as a deadly black ops squad tasked with defending the dwindling mutant race by any means necessary. Wolverine and his teammates all donned new variations on their traditional unifroms, one where all the color was replaced by stealthy blacks and greys.

It seems that Marvel's Wolverine isn't including a traditional version of Logan's iconic Tiger Stripe costume (though we have to assume it's coming eventually). For now, the closest option is this version, which pairs that beloved costume with the animated aesthetic of X-Men '97. You'll just have to deal with not hearing Cal Dodd's voice coming out of this character's mouth.

Like with the Spider-Man games, Insomniac's designers have come up with a couple of original designs for Logan to wear in the game. One is a bold black and yellow striped suit, and the other is an armored costume with a distinctive black and blue color scheme. We can only assume more original designs will be added to the game over time.

That's all the costumes confirmed to appear in Marvel's Wolverine so far. What suit do you most want to see in the game? Vote in our poll and let us know your thoughts in the comments below:

articles.title: Ninja Gaiden Legitimized the American Xbox Console for Japanese Developers
articles.summary: Itagaki-san had squeezed every bit of power and performance out of Microsoft’s fledgling console, and the result was what some people believe – including me and, more importantly, our resident action-game aficionado Mitchell Saltzman – is the single greatest pure action game ever made. You talk about aging well? It wasn’t just the combat, the precision controls, and the replayability that still hold up today. It’s all of that, but Ninja Gaiden even had native widescreen support back in 2004! When nobody had widescreen displays yet! We were all still on chonky 4:3 CRTs.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy.” In the run-up to Xbox’s 25th anniversary, he’ll be sharing his memories from the platform’s first quarter-century.

The Xbox was not always taken seriously – especially in its earliest days, and especially in Japan. “The Windows people? Making a console? They’re a software company.” No matter where you lived, if you were a gamer around the turn of the century, you remember that there was a lot to point and laugh at: the comically massive console. The absurdly large “Duke” controller (later replaced by the much better and smaller Controller S). It was… a lot.

And yes, Halo: Combat Evolved is the game that cemented Xbox’s place in the console industry. No one in their right mind would ever argue that. But it’s also true that up to that point in history, every console needed great games from the incredibly talented developers in Japan in order to survive and thrive. The Xbox, as the first major Western console, didn’t have that. Its early games, like the console itself, mostly came out of the West.

Until a developer named Tomonobu Itagaki, the head of Tecmo’s internal development group Team Ninja (who passed away last year), believed in the Xbox and the additional horsepower it could provide compared to the established industry giant Sony and its PlayStation 2. Itagaki brought his Tekken competitor, Dead or Alive, exclusively to the Xbox as a day-one launch title in November of 2001: Dead or Alive 3. Simply put, it kicked ass. The fighting game genre was an important one, and Xbox already had a fantastic example thanks to Itagaki-san and his Team Ninja crew.

I wasn’t much of a fighting game player back then, but buzz had been building for Itagaki’s next project: Ninja Gaiden, a revival of the beloved – and notoriously challenging – side-scrolling action game for arcades and, later, the NES. And when Itagaki-san brought an early build to the Official Xbox Magazine offices to show it to us, I couldn’t help but notice.

By now you’ve heard about Itagaki and his rockstar persona: the long hair, the sunglasses worn indoors, the black leather jacket and pants. The cigarettes. The dude put it out there, and with Dead or Alive 3 he had already backed it up. With Ninja Gaiden, he was about to take it to another level.

Through a translator, Itagaki-san told us all about Ninja Gaiden and the combat challenge it would offer. It was beautiful, it ran at 60 frames per second, and its combat was stunning just to watch, let alone play. And when it came out, it garnered universal praise and acclaim – which it deserved every bit of. We gave it a 9.6 out of 10 at OXM – then our highest score ever. IGN went with a 9.4 . Itagaki-san had squeezed every bit of power and performance out of Microsoft’s fledgling console, and the result was what some people believe – including me and, more importantly, our resident action-game aficionado Mitchell Saltzman – is the single greatest pure action game ever made . You talk about aging well? It wasn’t just the combat, the precision controls, and the replayability that still hold up today. It’s all of that, but it even had native widescreen support back in 2004! When nobody had widescreen displays yet! We were all still on chonky 4:3 CRTs.

Even Itagaki himself could never top Ninja Gaiden (though Ninja Gaiden 2 was pretty damn good anyway), but it didn’t matter. He had shown the Japanese development community that you could do incredible things on the Xbox. And though the Xbox ultimately failed in Japan, it wasn’t for a lack of trying (see what would come later, such as Blue Dragon, Lost Odyssey, Eternal Sonata, and more). And we’ll always have Ninja Gaiden.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: YouTube Star MrBeast Has Written a Book, Though There Are Conflicting Reports Of His Success
articles.summary: YouTuber MrBeast has co-written a novel — but the book has reportedly performed poorly in pre-order sales.
articles.body:
UPDATE: IGN has received fresh publishing information on MrBeast's book from a senior-level source with knowledge of the numbers, disputing the narrative that the project is on track to "bomb."

Indeed, presale figures are "beyond four digits" and "tracking well for a debut novel," IGN has been told. It's also understood that the marketing strategy for MrBeast's book is not focused specificially on driving pre-orders, as it's believed that the YouTube mega star's younger audience will likely pick up the novel after publication day — which is today.

The Most Dangerous Games is available, priced $35 for a hardcover copy. More details on its plot can be found in our original story, below.

ORIGINAL STORY: YouTube star Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, has co-written a novel — but the book has reportedly performed poorly in pre-order sales.

The Most Dangerous Games, Donaldson's thriller debut written in collaboration with Alex Cross author James Patterson, is currently "on track to be a historic bomb," according to news service Semafor , via The Hollywood Reporter .

A fictionalized version of a large-scale MrBeast survival game, the novel tells the story of 100 strangers who sign up for a contest to win a billion dollars. The only thing standing in their way? A series of deadly challenges that begin on the thinning ice of Antarctica — oh, and the deadly allegiances that form between the other players through the contest.

It all sounds a bit like Battle Royale meets Squid Game, which you would think would be a winning formula. But apparently there are concerns that the book's presales numbers "numbering in the four digits" is just a "tiny fraction of what th epublisher will need to justify Patterson's and YouTuber Jimmy Donaldson's hefty fees."

Herein, it seems, lies the problem. Because while the report lists The Most Dangerous Games as being "on track to be a historic bomb," presales in the single-digit thousands are typical for books of this kind, per a publishing source who spoke with IGN today. And time will tell how well the book sells over time, as Donaldson promotes it in YouTube videos, and as the lucrative end of year sales season nears. Indeed, the YouTuber has already appeared in a video titled "Read My Book, You Could Win $1,000,000," which should help sell a few more copies.

Still, publisher HarperCollins could be on the hook for a sizable sum regardless of how the book sells, depending on the advance paid to Donaldson and Patterson simply to secure the publishing rights and receive the manuscript. How much this was, we can but speculate.

The Best Comic Book or Original Graphic Novel of 2025

"A thousand strangers receive the invitation," reads a blurb for the novel. "One hundred make the cut. The Games begin in Antarctica, where one wrong step on the ice kills you, and they never let up: Shark water off a remote Chilean island, desert heat that cooks you where you stand, storm-battered peaks, and caves so black you cannot find your own hand. No rescue. No second chances. A billion dollars to whoever is still standing.

"Then the terrain stops being the thing that can kill you, and the other players start. Alliances turn into ambushes. Trust becomes the sharpest weapon. And somewhere above it all, a hidden voice is watching every move, testing, deciding who deserves to survive."

Image credit: Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images

articles.title: GTA Vice City Made Escaping Cop Land The Biggest Thrill
articles.summary: Remember Cop Land, the GTA Vice City level where you dressed up as cops to blow up a bomb? It was frustrating, but it was the start of a huge, ambitious shift for Grand Theft Auto.
articles.body:
It was supposed to be an easy job. Get in, set the detonators, get out, get paid. But now, with seemingly every fed in the state on my tail, it’s clear that Cop Land, one of GTA Vice City’s mid-game missions, is anything but an easy job.

You very possibly don’t like Cop Land. In fact, you might hate it . It is fiddly, easily failed, and messing up will send you right back to the start of its four-objective gauntlet. It requires wrangling the police’s uncooperative AI routines and infiltrating enemy territory, all while babysitting your partner in crime, Lance Vance. Oh, and you also have to survive a five-star wanted level chase through the city. It’s like the escort quest from hell… and it’s sort of brilliant.

To understand why something so frustrating can still be genuinely fantastic, we first need to rewind the clock. When Vice City arrived in late 2002, it made the earlier games – even the genre-defining GTA 3 that had launched just a year prior – look like primitive toys. It achieved its lofty ambition through a variety of avenues: a bigger, more interesting city; a wider variety of vehicles; a property management system; a better-written story; and, of course, a totally impeccable ‘80s vibe.

Arguably more interesting, if less even in its execution, was Vice City’s ambition to deliver more complex mission design than its predecessors. Until this point, GTA typically sent you out to achieve a single violent objective before flashing up the Mission Complete card and showering you with money. Vice City does admittedly have plenty of those, especially during its opening act, but as Tommy Vercetti’s journey takes him into the big leagues, the missions ask more and more of you, to varying degrees of success. One of the best examples of this ambition is Cop Land, which takes you on a journey of rapidly escalating stakes across the city’s Vice Point neighborhood.

Cop Land is the final mission in the Vercetti Estate arc. Tommy has just had notorious gangster Ricardo Diaz rubbed out of existence, and now he runs the most powerful criminal enterprise in the city. But things are far from rosy: with Diaz gone, many of the crime lord’s former business associates are refusing to pay protection money to the new guy in charge. Tommy sets out to intimidate his “clients” over a couple of missions, killing other gang members attempting to muscle in on his turf, as well as shattering the storefronts of the businesses that refuse to pay for protection. It’s a chain of missions with thematic consistency and escalating stakes – something Vice City’s older siblings can’t really boast about.

Unfortunately, a few broken windows won’t intimidate the owner of a coffee shop in the North Point Mall, so one of Tommy’s guys sets up a bomb to torch the place. But the wiring is cooked, and the mall is now locked down by the bomb squad. To destroy the evidence and save their new empire from crumbling before it’s even begun, Tommy and Lance have no other option than sneaking into cop land and detonating the bomb themselves.

To say the mall is “crawling with cops” is a bit of an understatement. The entire top-half of the Vice Point district becomes overrun with them, replacing all pedestrians and traffic with hordes of beat cops and lines of police cruisers. It’s an impressive use of asset switching to create a tense environment; the whole north tip of the island is now an impregnable fortress manned by doughnut munchers.

To get inside the mall, Tommy and Lance are going to have to disguise themselves as cops. This is the mission’s first objective, but in an impressive display of how dedicated Rockstar was to making Vice City feel like an authentic place where you could do whatever you wanted, you can completely ignore what you’re supposed to do and waltz into the mall wearing your Hawaiian shirt. You will face a wall of armed cops given full authority to open fire thanks to the five-star wanted level you trigger by trespassing the crime scene, so this is tantamount to suicide, but the fact that you can attempt it makes Vice City feel genuinely freeform and impressively reactive.

To see the mission through properly, you’ll need to acquire a couple of police uniforms, a process that demands you lure two officers into a garage so that you can beat them up and steal their clothes. Thankfully, the mall’s lockdown means there are more cops than you’ll ever need literally down the road from your lock-up. Frustratingly, actually getting them to give up their clothes is as fun as rubbing pepper spray in your eyes.

Since you need two uniforms, you need two cops to follow you into the garage. That means incurring more than a single wanted star, as minor crimes typically only send one officer after you. But causing a little more mayhem will dispatch multiple police cars to your location, which almost always screech to a halt right in front of the lock-up, preventing the garage door from shutting. If the door can’t drop, the cutscene that nets you the uniforms won’t trigger. Your only option is to endure the chaos as you reverse cars out of the driveway and encourage cops to follow you into the garage rather than take potshots at you from the other side of the street. You’re completely at the mercy of the police’s AI routines, making for a challenge that feels almost random – you could smoothly swipe the uniforms on the first attempt, or end up in a frustrating cycle of deaths and arrests.

With your disguises secured, you can move on to the next objective and approach the bomb. So long as you don’t do anything stupid, you can calmly walk through the mall to the coffee shop and step into the highlighted zone to fix the explosives. After that, it should just be a case of driving away from the scene.

In yet another example of your crew’s questionable talent for crime, the bomb is on a five-second fuse. Tommy and Lance are barely clear of the blast radius before the cafe is blown to smithereens (a detonation that permanently scars the map, a Rockstar trick that began in GTA 3 ). Very obviously the perpetrators of this very serious crime, the pair must now escape every cop in cop land, who have all suddenly become very trigger-happy thanks to the five-star wanted level you’ve earned for dabbling in activities adjacent to domestic terrorism.

Five stars is Vice City’s second-highest wanted level. It turns the police practically feral, completely disregarding any sense of road responsibility or personal safety in their pursuit of you. They use their cars not so much as battering rams, but as V6-powered homing missiles. So long as justice is served, they really don’t care about the cost.

But it’s not just the police who now stand in your way: SWAT teams are deployed across the city, arriving in armoured vans and rappelling from helicopters. The FBI also give chase in their armoured SUVs, their men armed with automatic weaponry. Getting out alive ain’t gonna be easy, so you’ve got to think about the escape before you even set one foot in the building.

Where you park your car before entering the mall is surprisingly vital to your success. The obvious place is at the mall’s main streetside door, but the coffee shop is on the opposite side of the shopping centre, so when the shit hits the fan, you’ll have to fight through a legion of armed officers to reach your getaway wheels. That’s why the smart decision is to park in the side alley that runs along the south side of the mall – you can actually leave your car right outside the exit that’s closest to the coffee shop. Post-detonation, you’ll be barely 10 yards away from your ticket out of here.

There’s another good reason to park by the south entrance. The alley contains arguably the most useful pick-up for this scenario: the Bribe, which lowers your wanted level by one star. That’ll take you down to four stars, removing the FBI from the hunt. It’s a canny placement from Rockstar, allowing anyone who spends a few minutes scoping out the joint to gain an almost immediate advantage in the mission’s final objective of escaping back to the Vercetti Estate.

But there’s still work to do: you need to survive the car chase home. Well, I say you – anyone who has a decent handle on Vice City’s driving will likely have little issue making it to Starfish Island, especially considering the most direct route back to the Vercetti Estate passes by a second Bribe, hidden where the road forks near the Vice Point Penthouse. But neither the route nor wanted level is the real issue here; your Achilles heel is Lance, who’s effectively a dead man’s switch for the mission failed screen.

If Lance snuffs it, it’s all over – go directly back to your last save, do not pass Go, do not collect the police uniforms that already took you five attempts to steal. And Lance is really, really good at dying. You’re fighting against the tinderbox that is two PS2-era AI systems grinding against each other – Lance’s primitive pathfinding means he can only barely follow you, and the “stop at all costs” aggression of the police means he’s constantly pulled into firefights he has no hope of winning. Your only option is to get him into a car as soon as possible and pray to god that the cops don’t shunt you off the road; if you ever need to switch cars, Lance is a guaranteed goner, either from the explosion of your wreck or the relentless gunfire that hails down as you hijack new wheels.

Ensure Lance survives the final chase and you’ll be rewarded with $10,000 and – more importantly – a regular income. You’ve successfully set up a protection ring, and money will gradually trickle in from your many clients for the remainder of the campaign. But the real reward is the satisfaction of completing one of the game’s most ambitious, flawed missions.

Vice City saw Rockstar’s first experiments in highly scripted, multi-stage missions. Today, these are the norm – it’s impossible to imagine GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 without their cinematic heists and dramatically escalating events. But the origins of these missions was a messy affair, as Rockstar suffered through the pain of making them work in a city sandbox that had previously been the stage for quests typically no more complicated than “drive to point X to kill person Y”. Cop Land is one of those awkward missions – it’s impossible to call it a triumph considering the fiddly nature of securing those uniforms and escorting Lance out of the hot zone.

But while some consider it one of the worst GTA missions ever, Cop Land often finds itself on lists of Vice City’s best moments, and it’s not hard to see why. Fooling the police with stolen uniforms is a singular high, and the against-all-odds escape is a car chase for the history books. It’s also a mission that embraces the many possibilities of an open world – you can completely bypass the car chase finale by parking a helicopter next to the mall and taking to the skies the moment things heat up. Cop Land is a brilliant example of Vice City at its most ambitious, and a reminder of why Rockstar’s groundbreaking PS2 era was so important for the entire medium.

Matt Purslow is IGN's Executive Editor of Features.

articles.title: Don't Worry, The Witcher 3 Saves Will Work With The Game's Remastered Upgrade — And There's Word on Achievements/Trophies, Too
articles.summary: The Witcher 3 developer CD Projekt has confirmed you'll be able to use your existing save files with the game's upcoming Remastered edition — and provided detail on Achievements and Trophies, too.
articles.body:
The Witcher 3 developer CD Projekt has confirmed you'll be able to use your existing save files with the game's generous upcoming Remastered edition — and provided detail on Achievements and Trophies, too.

Writing today via a post on X/Twitter, the studio said it had seen a number of fan questions over the game's forthcoming new edition, which will be awarded to existing owners of the game. This is even the case for Nintendo Switch owners upgrading to a copy of Remastered on Nintendo Switch 2, and free on all platforms.

"Good news: your current saves will work with the upgrade, so you can get back on the Path right where you left off," CD Projekt wrote. This is great news for lapsed fans who still haven't seen everything The Witcher 3 has to offer (and there is a lot on offer).

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Songs of the Past gamescom ONL 2026 Teaser Trailer - Screenshots

And, of course, it's worth remembering that the base game now includes access to its two expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine. You'll want to play both of those before the RPG's belated third expansion, Songs of the Past, launches in 2027.

There's more good news for achievement (and trophy) hunters, as progress toward any award unlocked so far will be tracked and continued in the game's Remastered edition. This is perhaps less of a surprise, if the upgraded game is treated simply as an update on supported platforms. Still, it's nice to have confirmed.

CD Projekt Red announced The Witcher 3 Remastered last week with a long list of additional features and technical improvements set to be included, such as the long-awaited cross-platform mod support, new quest tracking, immersive meditation, refined animations, UI improvements, a looting rework, and much, much more. Launching on September 29, the game's Remastered version will soon become its default offering, although there's also been a slight increase in price (presumably to reflect the fact that its expansions are now included).

For more on Songs of the Past, IGN has also taken a peek at one of its quests — and you can read more right now on what Geralt has in store next year.

articles.title: 'Did You Destroy My Favorite Game?': How the Heroes of Might and Magic 3 Community Is Guiding Ubisoft’s Reboot
articles.body:
Ubisoft just revealed a remake of 1999's Heroes of Might and Magic 3 at Gamescom, and one look at the trailer shows it goes far beyond a simple polish and port. Set to release in 2027 across console and PC, the new game will swap the original's isometric 2D view with a 3D world and add new content - a fresh prologue campaign and some fancy cinematics - and tweak the original mechanics to make the game more accessible, without diluting the gameplay.

IGN spoke to Jean-Felix Monin, Creative Director at Ubisoft China, about the project and how the still very dedicated Heroes of Might and Magic 3 fanbase has been a key part of shaping this new version.

"I would say for us, the intention behind this game was really, there's this community, there's this great game that people have been kind of asking for a remake of for years now, and so we really want to do right by them," he said.

"We had contact with some key people in the community, people that we had worked with on other transmedia stuff, such as the board game, people that we knew we trusted and were quite representative and well-known, and they came and did some consulting."

This helped the team navigate some of the big changes, like the huge change from 2D isometric to 3D, complete with dynamic weather and seasons, and served as a north star for any gameplay changes. "So, the goal for us was to be really clear on the gameplay first. The gameplay is considered a masterpiece. And it's true that when you play the game, you really realize that, oh, wow, it's magical," said Monin.

"We took the decision really early on to not touch the gameplay. So, all the systems, all the balancing, had to stay exactly the same. We thought that through that, that would actually also address the question of, 'Okay, did you destroy my favorite game?'" he explained.

"We couldn't destroy it because we didn't touch it. That part we really didn't touch. And then on top of that, it was really, 'What can we do without touching this to make sure that we bring more value?' So the graphics, obviously, and also some quality of life features that we've added to make sure that modern players wouldn't feel too lost, because it's still kind of a unique type of gameplay, and so it might be a bit of a gap for people to get into it."

He also explained the decision to add a new prologue campaign. "There were kind of two reasons why we came with this idea," he said. "One was there was a lack of a good tutorial, so the original game just like threw you in. So you have the manual, so I guess people in the day were okay to read the book to understand about the game, but this is not something people do too much now."

"And there had been a tutorial made before, but that wasn't great. So we really thought there was a real need to teach this game to new players. So, this is something we needed to take the time to create. At the same time, there were a bit of loose ends, I would say, that are non-clear in the narrative about what happens before Catherine gets to Erathia and to Antagarich, and we thought that could be a good moment actually to mesh both together, because it's the first thing you play, and so that kind of eases you into the story and the gameplay at the same time."

The original Heroes of Might and Magic 3 scored a 9 on IGN when it was released, with our review calling it a triumphant return for the series and urging players old and new to give it a shot. "If you've already bought and played Heroes of Might and Magic I and II, you'll definitely be happy with 3. And if you're new to this series, pick this one up and give it a try."

Monin had a similar hope. "I think the goal is for us to really talk to the fans with nostalgia, to really get the feeling that they had 20-plus years ago," he said. "And then from there, we think by proxy, there could be a lot of new people coming in."

Rachel Weber is the Head of Editorial Development at IGN and an elder millennial. She's been a professional nerd since 2006 when she got her start on Official PlayStation Magazine in the UK, and has since worked for GamesIndustry.Biz, Rolling Stone and GamesRadar. She loves horror, horror movies, horror games, Red Dead Redemption 2, and her Love and Deepspace boyfriends.

articles.title: The Big Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest Interview: Release Date, Clan Roles, Combat, and More
articles.summary: We got to speak with one of the developers behind Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest, who opened up about the team’s creative process and what it’s like bringing the Clans to life.
articles.body:
Erin Hunter’s Warrior Cats franchise is finally getting an officially licensed video game coming to all major platforms this fall. We got to speak with one of the developers behind the turn-based title, who opened up about the team’s creative process and what it’s like bringing the Clans to life.

As a lifelong fan of the Warrior Cats world, I couldn’t believe it when I got the chance to quiz the developers at Bamtang Games and the folks at Coolabi Group about Clans of the Forest, the upcoming turn-based role-playing game based on the four original clans of the Warriors book series.

I also get to be the one to happily break the news of its official launch date. Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest will release on October 23, 2026 on PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, Nintendo Switch, and Nintendo Switch 2.

Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest Official Screenshots

With that out of the way, let’s take a dive into my conversation with Adam Johnston, Creative Director at Bamtang Games, who assured me that his team is doing everything they can to stay true the the books’ lore — even to the point of bringing in community members to keep them on the right path.

IGN: The Warriors books are beloved by generations of fans. How does it feel being honored with the task of bringing this world to life?

Adam Johnston: Looking at the sheer scale of the world Erin Hunter built was a little intimidating at first. Once you realize just how many books, characters, and Clan dynamics exist, you understand the size of the mountain you're climbing. But as soon as our team jumped into the stories, that intimidation turned into excitement. We fell in love with the lore. Bringing it to life became a dream project for us. To make sure we get every detail right, we’ve had dedicated super fans working alongside us throughout development. They keep us honest and make sure we don't accidentally violate any sacred Clan traditions along the way. Having their feedback paired with our team's energy has been amazing. Our goal has been to craft something deeply authentic for readers who grew up with the series, while making it just as engaging for someone discovering Warriors for the first time. It's a huge responsibility, but we couldn't ask for a better world to build. If we have accidentally messed up the etiquette of a Gathering, we fully expect StarClan to strike us down.

IGN: Tell me a little bit about the production process for Clans of the Forest. Why a turn-based RPG? Was any inspiration taken from the Roblox game?

Adam Johnston: When you look at combat in the books, it isn't just cats slashing wildly at each other. It’s about stealth, positioning, and working as a team. A turn-based RPG made the most sense because it forces you to think strategically instead of just mashing buttons. It also let us build proper team battles and gives us a solid framework to make fights against badgers, foxes, or rival patrols actually work mechanically. Designing RPG combat for cats meant ditching standard spells. Instead, depth comes from shifting combat Stances. Every move you make alters your stance mid-fight, turning battles into a tactical game of reading your opponent and predicting their next move before they strike. As for Roblox, tons of respect to that community. They showed everyone years ago just how badly fans wanted to roleplay in this world. We're building a structured RPG rather than an open sandbox, but seeing their success gave us a lot of confidence that the appetite was definitely there.

IGN: Why did you make the choice to let players create their own cat, rather than play through the story as one of the established cats in the series?

Adam Johnston: If you ask almost any Warriors fan, the first thing they did after reading the books was figure out what their own warrior name would be and which Clan they belonged to. Self-expression is a huge part of why people fall in love with this universe in the first place. If we forced you to play as Firestar or another established character, you’d just be running through a story where you already know how everything turns out. Letting players create their own cat completely changes the game. It gives you incredible replayability, because every new cat you make comes with a different Clan, look, stat setup, and personality. Over time, you aren't just playing a single campaign. You're building your own personal legacy across the forest, populating the world with your own web of stories, rivalries, and characters across multiple playthroughs.

IGN: How important was cat customization to you? (As a kid who absolutely designed their own Warrior Cat OC, believe me, I get the appeal. Haha!)

Adam Johnston: Everyone who read these books had a notebook somewhere filled with their own custom cat designs. We knew if we didn't give players deep customization, we'd be missing the entire point of making a Warriors game. We wanted to make sure you could customize initial visuals like pelt patterns and eye colors, but also see your cat change as they get older. Your cat will start out as a cute apprentice and eventually end up looking like a grizzled veteran who has seen way too many badgers. On top of that, we tied identity directly into mechanics. Your Clan, level, and training shape your base stats, while the choices you make along your journey determine the moves you learn. That way, your cat actually grows up and lives a different story in the forest each time.

IGN: Will players get to choose certain roles, like being a Medicine Cat? Why or why not?

Adam Johnston: We anchored the player's path in the warrior ranks because every Clan needs a clear leader to face the prophecy, and we wanted the player to be that hero. While being a Medicine Cat is a fantasy for a lot of fans, their duty in the lore is healing and spiritual guidance, not tactical dueling or Clan leadership. The emotional climax across all four Sagas relies on you standing at the head of your Clan during its most dangerous hour. To give players a Hero's Journey, we wanted your choices to directly affect Clan politics and leadership. That said, Medicine Cats still play an important role in your journey. They are central to the story, spiritual guidance, and survival of your Clan, even if you aren't the one dispensing catmint yourself.

IGN: The Warriors books are known for being quite brutal, despite their young audience. Was the inclusion of any blood and gore discussed for this game?

Adam Johnston: We discussed this early on because the books are famous for their fierce battles. But for us, it wasn't about showing blood, it was about honoring the resilience of a warrior. We designed stylized visual scars that feel earned after tough encounters, avoiding anything graphic or scary. Giving players a toggle to turn those scars on or off in the settings was a crucial decision for us: it respects different age groups, sensory comfort, and player agency without diluting the dramatic tension of big important fights.

IGN: Is any DLC planned after the game's launch?

Adam Johnston: Right now, we are focused on the launch of the game. Any updates or plans for additional content will be addressed later.

IGN: And finally, do you have a message to the fans about what they can expect from Clans of the Forest?

Adam Johnston: The books don't pull punches. You've got dog packs, vicious badger fights, and some genuinely heavy character deaths. We knew we couldn't make a sanitized version of the forest, because treating this universe with respect means honoring those actual stakes. At the same time, we didn't want gratuitous gore just for shock value. Our goal was to match the emotional weight of the books rather than turn it into a total splatterfest. You’ll feel the tension of combat, and your cat will pick up scars as they age, but the focus is on story and consequences of choices. Get ready to prove you're warrior material, not just a soft kittypet.

I also got the chance to quiz a few members of the Coolabi Group, a British media company that has owned the rights to the Warrior franchise since 2012. Specifically, I got to chat with Nick Cooke, Director of Product Development, as well as Jordan Long and Stephanie Lane Elliot from Coolabi’s Editorial team.

Jordan Long: I have been reading the books since 2005, when I was just a kid in elementary school and the Warrior Cats series only had eight published books to its name. Now there are hundreds of books, graphic novel adaptations, multiple lines of merchandise, a television series in development - and now the upcoming game. It has been absolutely incredible to be a part of creating this newest chapter in the Warrior Cats story. It feels like reaching back in time and gifting myself the game I always dreamed of as a child, and I hope the players feel the love that was put into this, as a gamer and as a lifelong fan of the books.

IGN: What was the most important aspect from the books that you felt you just had to get right in the game?

Jordan Long: One of the most important things we wanted this game to do for fans was to really let them feel that they weren’t just playing a video game with a Warrior Cats logo slapped onto it, but truly getting to play through a story that felt authentic to the world of Warrior Cats. Not just the mechanics of hunting and fighting and designing their cat, but getting to have the experience of living in the world of the Clans, facing the sort of heavy destiny that many of the characters in the books have been presented with and having the choice of how they want to approach it. We feel that the four stories we’ve put together for the four Clans feel authentic to the world of the books - tales of prophecies, hardship, courage, and the bonds forged both within and outside of your Clan that determine the kind of warrior you become.

Stephanie Lane Elliot: We wanted to make sure the game gave a realistic view of what it feels like to live in the Clans, the weight of the choices a warrior makes every day, and how those choices can impact not only their lives but the lives of all their Clanmates.

IGN: The Warriors books are known for being quite brutal, despite their young audience. Was the inclusion of any blood and gore discussed for this game? Why or why not?

Nick Cooke: We talked a lot about how to bring battling into the gameplay in a way that felt true to the Warrior Cats world, while also being appropriate for a broad audience. We were very conscious of the sensitivity around violence, particularly given the age range of the books’ audience, but we also wanted the combat to feel meaningful and engaging.

The turn-based battle system gives players the opportunity to really step into the role of a warrior. You can hunt prey, defend yourself against predators, and fight alongside your Clan against rival Clans. We felt that focusing on strategy, character abilities, and the excitement of the battle itself allowed us to capture that sense of danger and adventure without relying on graphic blood or gore. By having multi-character battles, particularly battles between Clans, is also a big part of making the game feel like the world of Warrior Cats. It gives players the chance to experience those larger-scale conflicts and, ultimately, feel like they’re truly part of their Clan.

IGN: Fans seem to be equal parts cautious and excited for both the Clans of the Forest game and the upcoming animated series. Do you have any words for the fanbase as to what they can expect from the franchise under Coolabi’s purview?

Nick Cooke: Warrior Cats will celebrate its 25th anniversary in 2028, and over those 25 years we have strived to support our extraordinary global fanbase who have made the world of Warrior Cats their own. With more than 90 million books sold and the Roblox game rapidly approaching one billion plays, it’s clear that the appetite for this world is stronger than ever — and there is still a lot more to come.

Our ambition is to continue expanding the ways fans can experience and participate in the world of Warrior Cats, while always respecting what has made the franchise so special to them. Ahead of the animated series which is slated to premiere in 2028, we’ll be launching a number of digital and social media programs with a variety of content, designed to give fans new ways to engage with the characters, stories and wider world. These will sit alongside our continued investment in publishing and our expanding consumer products programme, helping us build a broader digital presence for the franchise.

We also recognise that the Warrior Cats community has been creating, imagining and expanding this world for years. Emmy Award-winning director Rodrigo Blaas, who is directing the animated series, spoke recently about the incredible creativity of the fans and the responsibility that comes with bringing the books to animation:

“People and fans have been animating these books on their own time, in their bedrooms, at their desks, because they were not going to wait for somebody to make it official. Many of those works are beautiful. We have watched a lot of it. This is the first time these books are officially becoming an animated series. So we know we are not the first people who tried to bring this world to animated life. We are just the first ones who get to do it at this scale, and we do not take that lightly.” This really captures how we feel about the future of Warrior Cats. We know we’re building on something that already means a huge amount to millions of people. The goal is not simply to make more Warrior Cats content, but to create new experiences that give existing fans something to be excited about while welcoming a new generation into the Clans.
